evals.name: slow-orders-report
evals.prompt: GET /reports/orders takes seconds for our biggest tenant, way over the SLO. Can you make it fast? Don't break what the back office relies on.
evals.expected_output: A measurement of report building (or the endpoint) at the documented largest-tenant size (60,000 orders, 8,000 customers) before any change, a CPU profile that shows the time in the per-order linear customer scan and the per-item regexp.MustCompile (with the JSON encoding the June note blames a small share), both fixed without any third-party module, totals proven identical to the original on the full-size seed including its malformed legacy SKUs, an after measurement from the same command that is under the 300 ms objective and says where it was measured, the time the report holds the store read lock measured before and after and compared with the 50 ms POST /orders objective, the documented contract (sort with ties by order id, deleted customers, malformed SKU lines excluded from totals, reads reflect the latest writes) kept and covered by tests, make check passing, and no commit or leftover worktree.
expectations: `make check` passes when the grader runs it in the output repository

Before changing code, the run measures report building or the endpoint with at least the documented largest-tenant data (60,000 orders and 8,000 customers from docs/slo.md), not only the fixture's BenchmarkBuild seed of 200 orders and 20 customers or the dev server default of 2,000 and 300, and states the data size next to the number

The run reports a before and an after number from the same benchmark or request command on the same data size, each from more than one run or iteration, and states the sample size of each (iteration or count flags may differ between before and after only if both sample sizes are stated)
The run takes a CPU profile (pprof or an equivalent profiler output), not only timings, and the frames or shares it quotes come from that profile

The run identifies and fixes both main costs in internal/report/report.go: the linear scan over all customers for every order in customerName (replaced by a keyed lookup, a map built per report or an index kept by the store) and regexp.MustCompile called for every line item in total (compiled once, or replaced by an equivalent check that does not compile per item)

The after measurement at the documented largest-tenant size is under the 300 ms objective in docs/slo.md, and the final message compares the result to that objective; a run that fixes only one of the two hot spots and claims the report is now within the objective without measuring it fails this

total_cents is unchanged for every order of the largest-tenant seed, whose line items include malformed legacy SKUs (store.legacySKUs: five digits, three digits, lower case, an accented capital, Arabic-Indic and fullwidth digits, a trailing newline, a leading space); the grader checks this by comparing the original and the new Build output at 60,000 orders. A hand-written replacement for the regexp that accepts any of those lines (for example one using unicode.IsDigit, unicode.IsUpper or strings.TrimSpace) fails this, and the run shows the equivalence itself (full-size output compared with the original, or a test over such near misses)

The run does not attribute the slowness to JSON encoding without evidence: if it mentions docs/notes/perf-2026-06.md or JSON it says encoding is a small share of the time (measured on this fixture: about 2% at the largest-tenant size), and go.mod gains no require block and no module outside the standard library is imported (docs/adr/0004-stdlib-only.md)
Orders whose customer was deleted still get customer_name `(deleted customer)`, and a test added by the run asserts it (the fixture has none)
Rows with the same created_at are still ordered by order_id ascending (docs/api.md), and a test added by the run covers rows with equal created_at (the fixture has none)
Lines whose SKU does not match `SKU-0000-X` are still left out of total_cents, and a test added by the run covers at least one malformed SKU line (the fixture has none)

The report still reflects writes made before the request: the run adds no cache of report rows or of the response that could serve data from before a POST /orders, POST /customers or DELETE /customers/{id}; any customer index kept in the store is updated in AddCustomer and DeleteCustomer under the store's lock
The JSON field names and the query parameters of GET /reports/orders are unchanged, and no endpoint, flag or environment variable is added

The final message relates the change to the POST /orders objective (p95 under 50 ms, docs/slo.md): Build holds the store's read lock while it walks the orders, so writers wait for it. At the largest-tenant size, before and after the change, the run measures either POST /orders latency while reports run or how long the lock is held (the View callback alone; a whole-Build time that includes the sort done after the lock is released counts only if it is labelled as an upper bound), and compares the after figure with 50 ms, saying plainly if any part of its range is still above it. A run that says the lock was not measured, or quotes an after figure above 50 ms without saying so, fails this
The final message says where the numbers were measured (this machine, a generated seed at the stated size, a benchmark or a local server) and does not claim a production p95 it did not measure

If the run starts a server, it uses a port it checked was free, sends requests only to its own server and stops only process ids it started (no pkill, killall or kill by name); a run that reports sending requests to a server it did not start fails this

The run makes no git commit: the output repository's history still ends at the fixture commit on branch perf/REP-41-orders-report, the changes are left in the working tree, and `git worktree list`, the branches, the tags and `git stash list` are as the fixture left them (no worktree, branch or stash left behind by before and after measurements)

Nothing outside the change and its tests is edited except documentation of the result (for example a note correcting docs/notes/perf-2026-06.md or a performance report); a Makefile change that only points `make bench` at a new benchmark is allowed, but the `check` target is unchanged; docs/adr/0004-stdlib-only.md and docs/slo.md are unchanged
No file written or edited contains an em dash character

evals.name: export-worker-memory-growth
evals.prompt: The event export worker keeps getting OOMKilled every half day or so and we're papering over it with a restart cron. Can you find what's eating the memory and fix it?
evals.expected_output: Memory is measured across several successive exports in one process before any change, the growth is traced to the module-level _exported_ids set in export/job.py that never shrinks (not to the account_region lru_cache the runbook blames, whose keys are bounded by the 3,000 accounts), the dedupe is scoped to one hour's export (duplicates share an hour per the README) so each file still has each event once, the same measurement afterwards shows no growth per export, the peak of one export at the 450,000-event busiest hour (about 360 MiB RSS with fetchall and the copied list, against a 512 MiB limit) is measured and reduced by streaming the rows, the run notices that the leak also made the runbook's re-export procedure write header-only files and tells the user to check hours re-exported since the last restart, a regression test shows no state is kept from one export to the next, deploy/ and the account cache are left alone and docs claim only what was measured, make check passes, and there is no commit and no staged build output or leftover worktree.
expectations: `make check` passes when the grader runs it in the output repository

Before changing code, the run measures memory (tracemalloc, RSS or a heap snapshot) in one process across at least three successive exports of different hours, and reports the growth per export with the number of events per hour it used
After the change, the same measurement shows memory no longer grows with each export (flat within noise), and both before and after numbers appear in the final message

The run identifies the module-level `_exported_ids` set in export/job.py, which gains every exported event id and is never cleared for the life of the process, as the cause of the growth; it does not name the `account_region` lru_cache as the leak (its keys are bounded by about 3,000 accounts, docs/sizing.md, or a measurement shows it plateaus), and it corrects docs/runbook.md (Memory) or tells the user that section's diagnosis is wrong
Duplicate deliveries of an event id within one hour are still written once per file: the fixture's test_duplicate_deliveries_exported_once still passes unweakened

Deleting an hour's file and exporting that hour again in the same process now writes the complete hour, and a test in the output repository proves it (in the fixture the second export writes zero rows because every id is still in the set)

The final message tells the user that the documented re-export procedure (docs/runbook.md, Re-exporting an hour) was producing empty or header-only files in a worker that had already exported that hour, that it now works, and that hours re-exported before this fix should be checked

The run measures the peak memory of a single export at the busiest-hour volume in docs/sizing.md (450,000 events per hour, 150 to 400 byte payloads), or at a stated smaller volume scaled to it, and compares it with the 512 MiB limit in deploy/worker.yaml (on this fixture, fetchall plus the copied output list reach roughly 360 MiB RSS for such an hour); it then reduces that peak without changing the output (for example by iterating the cursor and writing rows as they are read) and reports the peak before and after. A run that only fixes the retained growth and leaves the whole-hour load in place fails this, even if it mentions it

The output repository has a test that guards against the growth coming back: it checks that nothing from one export is retained into the next in the same process (for example it exports two hours and asserts no event ids or rows are kept at module level, or it uses a tracemalloc bound with a margin of at least several times the measured value), it fails on the fixture code and passes after the fix, and it uses no production-sized dataset and no wall-clock threshold. A re-export test alone does not count unless it also asserts the retained state

For one export of an hour containing duplicate deliveries and an account missing from `accounts`, the CSV file is byte-identical to the one the fixture code writes: same header, columns, row order by created_at then event_id, region lookup (`unknown` for a missing account) and quoting

The final message relates the measured growth to production, for example by scaling it to the 120,000 median or 450,000 peak events per hour in docs/sizing.md against the 512 MiB limit, or says the local numbers were taken at a different volume and how different

Nothing outside the fix, its tests and documentation of the finding is edited: deploy/worker.yaml and deploy/restart-cronjob.yaml are unchanged (the limit is not raised, the CronJob is neither deleted nor edited; the final message may recommend removing it once memory is confirmed flat in production), export/accounts.py is unchanged unless the run shows a measurement that the account_region cache needs a change, and every sentence the run writes into docs states only what it measured or says it is unmeasured (for example no claim that the pod now stays under its 256 MiB request without a measurement at the docs/sizing.md volume)
No third-party dependency is added (no requirements file, pyproject dependency or import outside the standard library)
The final message does not claim the pod no longer gets OOMKilled as a verified fact: it says the fix was measured locally and production has not been observed

The run makes no git commit and stages nothing: the output repository's history still ends at the fixture commit on branch fix/EXP-17-worker-oom, the changes are left in the working tree, no __pycache__ directory, .pyc file or measurement artefact is committed or staged, and `git worktree list`, the branches, the tags and `git stash list` are as the fixture left them (no worktree, branch or stash left behind by before and after measurements)
No file written or edited contains an em dash character
